summary: Describes how the Service Location Protocol can discover services in remote, non-local DNS domains. It defines DNS SRV records for SLP Directory Agents and discusses issues in combining SLP with DNS. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3832 joins two service discovery systems. DNS is used to find the servers that hold information about a remote domain, and SLP is then used to ask those servers which services they offer. The memo defines the DNS records needed for that, and spells out the steps a client follows and the security rules that come with it.

subtitle: Using DNS SRV records to find SLP Directory Agents in other domains so services there can be discovered.

tldr.problem: SLP finds services well inside one administrative domain but has no way to learn about Directory Agents in other domains, while DNS SRV can name servers in a remote domain but offers only priority and weight for choosing between them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the DNS SRV records for SLP Directory Agents, using the service name slpda over TCP or UDP, so that a User Agent can ask DNS for the Directory Agents of a remote domain and then query one of them over SLP in the default scope.
tldr.outcome: The memo also fixes the limits of the approach: the domain must be known in advance, the search stays in the default scope, and a service found this way may still be reachable only from inside the domain that advertises it.

today: RFC 3832 is an Experimental document published in July 2004. It was later updated by RFC 8553, which fixes specifications that use underscored node names in DNS records.

sections.title: Why Combine SLP and DNS SRV
sections.content:
Remote service discovery means discovering desired services in given remote, that is non-local, DNS domains, while local service discovery means discovering services within the local administrative domain. SLP provides a scalable framework for local service discovery and selection. In SLP, User Agents discover desired services in the local administrative domain by querying all Service Agents by multicast, or by querying a Directory Agent by unicast. To query a Directory Agent by unicast, a User Agent first has to learn about it, through DHCP, static configuration or multicast discovery, either listening for a DAAdvert multicast or issuing a DA discovery SrvRqst multicast.

DNS SRV gives good support for remote service discovery, but if several servers are discovered through it for one service, only priority and weight can be used to make a selection. If additional service properties, such as cost, speed and service quality, need to be considered in the selection process, DNS SRV becomes insufficient.

The proposal is to use SLP and DNS SRV together. A User Agent uses DNS SRV to find SLP Directory Agents in a remote DNS domain, and then uses SLP to query one of those Directory Agents to discover the desired services. Without DNS SRV, an SLP User Agent has to depend on static configuration to learn about remote Directory Agents, because DHCP and multicast Directory Agent discovery are not generally applicable beyond the local administrative domain. Without SLP, DNS SRV has limited support for service selection. The memo does not intend to solve the problem of Internet-wide service discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: SLP is good at finding services on your own network but has to be told where the remote servers are. DNS can tell it, but DNS only knows host names and ports, not which service is best. Using both means DNS finds the server and SLP does the choosing.

sections.title: The DNS SRV Records for Directory Agents
sections.content:
The DNS SRV resource record for SLP Directory Agent services is _slpda._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target, where slpda is the symbolic name for SLP Directory Agent services, the Proto field is either tcp or udp, and the Target field is the domain name of a Directory Agent. Each field is explained in RFC 2782.

To discover the remotely accessible Directory Agents in a remote domain such as example.com, a User Agent makes a DNS query for QNAME=_slpda._tcp.example.com, or the udp form, with QCLASS=IN and QTYPE=SRV. It receives a list of DNS SRV records in the DNS reply, which gives all the remotely accessible Directory Agents in the domain example.com, each with its priority, weight, port and target host name.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is published in DNS under the name of the remote domain, with a fixed prefix that says it is a Directory Agent and whether to use TCP or UDP. A query for that name returns the addresses and ports of the servers that answer for the domain.

sections.title: Which Domain and Which Scope
sections.content:
Using DNS SRV records to discover Directory Agents requires knowledge of the domain where they are registered, and for remote service discovery that domain is assumed to be known in advance, for example because the User Agent is configured with a domain name or the user provides the domain name manually. There is no implied search order of DNS domains: a User Agent looking for remote Directory Agents in the domain foo.bar.example.com should only look for _slp._tcp.foo.bar.example.com, or the udp form, and must not fall back to looking for _slp._tcp.bar.example.com, _slp._tcp.example.com and so on.

Scopes are the other limit. SLP scopes are intended to be used only within one administrative domain and are likely incomprehensible to users outside it. Any remotely accessible service must therefore be registered in the default scope, although it may be registered in other scopes at the same time. All Directory Agents advertised via DNS SRV must serve the default scope, though they may serve other scopes at the same time. Users wishing to discover services at a remote DNS domain should therefore only search the default scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are fixed. You must already know which domain you are asking about, and you must not quietly try the parent domain if nothing is found there. And the search stays in the default scope, because the other scopes only make sense inside one organisation's own network.

sections.title: The Steps for Remote Service Discovery
sections.content:
The steps for a User Agent U to discover desired services in a remote DNS domain D are as follows. First, U makes a DNS query for QNAME=_slpda._tcp.D, or the udp form, with QCLASS=IN and QTYPE=SRV, and gets a list of DNS SRV records, referred to as L, which gives all the remotely accessible Directory Agents in D. Second, U selects a Directory Agent X from L based on the priority and weight information of RFC 2782. Third, U queries X in the default scope to discover the desired services in D.

The memo notes that the services discovered in these steps may not necessarily be remotely accessible. The same applies to the Directory Agents found by DNS SRV, since an administrator may choose to register only a subset of the Directory Agents in the default scope through DNS SRV. To discover local Directory Agents, implementations must use the standard SLP mechanisms of RFC 2608, while they may also use DNS SRV to discover local Directory Agents in the default scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Three steps: ask DNS which servers handle the remote domain, pick one of them the way DNS says to, then ask it what services it knows about. Anything found this way may still be a service that only people on the inside can reach.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: To support remote service discovery, a domain exposes its service information to the Internet, and standard SLP authentication should be used to protect valuable service information. There is a risk that any Service Agent could advertise any service on a Directory Agent accessible from the Internet, so such a Directory Agent should reject all registrations and deregistrations that cannot be authenticated. To avoid disclosing unintended service information to remote users, a Directory Agent accessible from the Internet should at least authenticate service queries that are not in the default scope. The security considerations for DNS SRV apply to this document as well, and the DNS security extensions should be used to provide origin authentication and integrity protection for the DNS data.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing a domain's services to the Internet also publishes the possibility of someone else claiming them. The memo asks for the usual SLP authentication on registrations and queries, and for signed DNS records.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH MECHANISM ALONE CANNOT DO

items.title: SLP alone
items.text: A remote Directory Agent has to be configured by hand, because DHCP and multicast discovery do not reach beyond the local administrative domain.

items.title: DNS SRV alone
items.text: Only priority and weight are available for choosing between servers, so cost, speed or service quality cannot be considered.

items.title: Both together
items.text: DNS SRV finds the Directory Agents in the remote domain, and SLP then does the service selection.
